continuation_en:
And if what is in our hands is better than what is in yours, you will have joined us in our affair and taken your share from it. So Allah—mighty and exalted—revealed, “Say: O disbelievers.”

Abu Ṣāliḥ related from Ibn ʿAbbās that they said to the Messenger of Allah: “If you would touch some of these gods, we would believe you.” Gabriel then came down to the Prophet with this surah. They despaired of winning him over and harmed him and his companions.

The definite article in “the disbelievers” refers to known persons, even though it has a generic form because it qualifies the vocative expression. The address concerns those whom Allah knew would die in disbelief. It is therefore particular while expressed in general wording. Al-Māwardī reported a similar explanation: the surah was revealed as an answer, and “the disbelievers” means a particular group, not every disbeliever, since some later believed and worshipped Allah, while others died or were killed in disbelief. Those latter persons are the addressees intended here.

Abū Bakr ibn al-Anbārī said that one who attacked the Qur’an proposed reading, “Say to those who disbelieve: I do not worship what you worship,” and claimed this was the correct form. He called this a fabrication against the Lord of the worlds, a weakening of the surah’s meaning, and a nullification of its purpose: Allah enabled His Prophet to abase the polytheists by addressing them directly with a reproachful form and binding them to what every intelligent person would disdain. The wording they proposed is already contained in the meaning of the received reading, while the received reading adds an implication absent from their alteration. Its meaning is: “Say to those who disbelieve: O disbelievers.” In Arabic, when someone says, “Say to Zayd: come to us,” the meaning is, “Say to Zayd: O Zayd, come to us.” The received reading therefore includes everything in their proposed wording, while their alteration loses the finer expression and more forceful meaning. The Messenger would confront them in their assembly and say, “O disbelievers,” although he knew they were angered by being ascribed to disbelief and included among its people; yet he was guarded and protected from their laying a hand on him or harming him. Whoever does not recite “Say: O disbelievers” as Allah revealed it removes one of the Prophet’s signs. Muslims should not rush into such a thing or deliberately diminish the distinctions Allah granted and honored him with.

As for the repetition, it has been said that it serves to emphasize the complete cutting off of their hopes, just as one says, “By Allah, I will not do such a thing,” and then, “By Allah, I will not do it.” Most specialists in meanings said that the Qur’an was revealed in the language of the Arabs, whose usages include repetition for emphasis and clarification, just as they also use abbreviation for lightness and concision. Moving from one expression to another is more effective for an orator or speaker than remaining confined to a single expression. Examples include: “Which of your Lord’s favors will you both deny?”, “Woe that Day to the deniers,” “No indeed; they will soon know—again, no indeed; they will soon know,” and “With hardship comes ease; indeed, with hardship comes ease.” All of this is for emphasis. A speaker may likewise say, “Shoot, shoot,” or “Hurry, hurry.” An example is the Prophet’s statement in the sound hadith: “I do not permit it; again, I do not permit it. Fāṭimah is only a part of me,” transmitted by Muslim. Al-Qurṭubī then cites several lines of Arabic poetry as further examples of emphatic repetition.

It has also been said that the repeated clauses correspond exactly to their proposal: “You worship our gods and we worship your God; then we worship our gods and we worship your God; then you worship our gods and we worship your God, continuing forever, one year and then another.” Every part of what they proposed was answered with its opposite—that this would never occur.
